messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Firefighter
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 62

Ahmad, a 37-year-old Middle Eastern firefighter, has been navigating the challenges of life with persistent anxiety and intrusive thoughts since he was stalked by a former colleague over a year ago. The stalking began shortly after Ahmad had reported his colleague's unethical behavior at work to their superior. Since then, Ahmad’s sense of safety has been shattered. Ahmad wakes up each morning feeling on edge, as if he is waiting for something bad to happen again. He often checks the locks on his front door multiple times before leaving for work and frequently double-checks the windows in the house to ensure they are secure. His wife, Leila, notices that Ahmad seems jumpy and easily startled; even a sudden noise from outside can cause him to flinch. At work, Ahmad has found himself struggling with concentration during training sessions and while on emergency calls. He feels like he’s always scanning his surroundings for potential threats or signs of the stalker’s presence. On one occasion, he mistook a fellow firefighter for the stalker when they were dressed similarly in their uniforms. This experience left him feeling embarrassed but also relieved that it was not his former colleague. Ahmad often wakes up in the middle of the night with nightmares about being chased or confronted by his stalker. In these dreams, he sees the same piercing gaze and hears the same threatening words that plagued him during the stalking period. When he wakes up sweating and trembling, Leila tries to comfort him but Ahmad sometimes pushes her away, feeling too vulnerable in those moments. His memories of the stalking have become intrusive, popping into his head at unexpected times. While driving home from work one day, a passing car with tinted windows triggered a flashback. He immediately felt trapped and overwhelmed by the same fear he experienced when he was being stalked. Ahmad had to pull over and take deep breaths until the panic subsided. The stalking has also affected his relationship with Leila. Ahmad often expresses feelings of guilt for putting her in danger, as the stalker once made a veiled threat against her. He tries to keep their daily activities unpredictable so that the stalker cannot anticipate where they will be. This unpredictability, however, causes tension and frustration between them. Ahmad’s job as a firefighter has become more challenging due to his PTSD symptoms. The adrenaline rush on emergency calls used to energize him, but now it triggers hypervigilance and anxiety. He often finds himself scanning the crowds for any signs of danger, which distracts him from focusing on the immediate tasks at hand. Despite his struggles, Ahmad tries to maintain a facade of normalcy. At work, he jokes with colleagues and takes part in training exercises as if nothing is wrong. But underneath this façade, he feels isolated and disconnected from others. He finds it difficult to trust anyone fully, especially after being betrayed by someone he thought was a friend. Leila has noticed that Ahmad spends more time at home than before, often avoiding social outings or even just casual walks around the neighborhood. He mentions feeling exhausted all the time and less motivated to engage in activities they used to enjoy together. Leila worries about him but also understands his need for security. Ahmad’s PTSD symptoms have started to affect his physical health as well. He has developed insomnia, often tossing and turning until late at night, plagued by images of the stalker. This lack of sleep makes it hard for him to stay alert and focused during work shifts, which in turn exacerbates his anxiety about making mistakes on the job. Despite these challenges, Ahmad continues to go to work each day, determined not to let fear control his life entirely. He finds solace in talking with Leila about his feelings and occasionally confides in a few trusted colleagues at the fire station. While he has considered seeking professional help, the thought of opening up about his experiences still feels daunting. Ahmad’s story is one of resilience amid ongoing trauma. His daily life remains marked by the lingering effects of the stalking, but he continues to seek ways to cope and maintain some semblance of normalcy in his relationships and career.
